turns.prompt_text: I've been writing a lot of shell scripts lately in the fish shell. While I like the ability to automate and create shortcuts, I strongly dislike the language. I really dislike how intricate and unique each package is, and how everything changes and churns and crumbles all the time. And the ground is always breaking from beneath the feet. It is because of this I wish that there was a higher language. I'm sure many people have tried to do it. It's something where you don't want to unify anything at all, because this ecosystem is chaotic. But you do want to create some order in some places.
turns.response_html:
It sounds like you've hit the exact wall that drives many engineers crazy. Shell scripting (even in a cleaner shell like Fish) fundamentally amounts to string manipulation and taping together disparate CLI tools, each with their own arcane flag conventions, breaking changes, and shifting syntax. You aren't just fighting the language; you're fighting an inherently chaotic ecosystem.

The idea of a "higher language" for system automation—one that brings order without trying to fruitlessly rewrite the entire open-source world—is a problem some brilliant developers have tackled.

Here is a breakdown of how the industry has tried to solve this, categorizing the approaches by how they try to bring order to the chaos.

1. Type-Safe / Structured Shells (The Data-Centric Approach)

Instead of treating everything as a raw stream of text (bytes/strings), these languages force tools to output structured data (like JSON or objects). This eliminates the "crumbling ground" of a tool subtly changing its whitespace output and breaking your awk or string split logic.

  • Nushell (nu): This is currently the frontrunner in this space. It feels like a modern shell but treats everything as a structured table. If you run ls, you don't get lines of text; you get a robust data structure you can filter, sort, and query like a database.
  • Elvish: Another modern shell that introduces real data types (lists, maps) and namespaces. It aims for high predictability—the ground doesn't shake because the language constructs are explicitly scoped and structurally sound.

2. Embedded Shells in Robust Languages (The "Wrapper" Approach)

If you don't want to learn an esoteric new shell language, the other alternative is to bring the power of a mature, general-purpose language down to the system level, wrapping the chaos of CLI execution in clean syntax.

  • ZX (by Google): If you know JavaScript/TypeScript, zx is incredibly powerful. It allows you to write scripts in Node.js but embeds bash scripting inside template literals. It automatically handles escaping, piping, and error handling safely. 
    // Example of ZX bringing order to chaos
let count = parseInt(await $`ls -1 | wc -l`);
  • Plumbum (Python): For Python devs, Plumbum turns CLI programs into local Python objects. Instead of dealing with subprocess.Popen nightmares, you can pipe commands using standard Python syntax (ls["-a"] | grep["pattern"]), giving you Python's robust error handling and type checking over raw CLI tools.

3. Domain-Specific Configuration Languages (The Declarative Approach)

If the scripts you are writing are designed to put the system into a specific state (e.g., installing packages, configuring files, symlinking dotfiles), the "highest" languages don't script the actions—they declare the state.

  • Nix / NixOS: This is the ultimate "stop the ground from breaking" tool. Nix treats system configuration as a pure, functional language. Packages are deterministic and isolated. If a package update breaks something on a traditional system, Nix avoids this entirely by ensuring dependencies never conflict or bleed into each other. The learning curve is steep, but it offers absolute immunity to ecosystem churn.
  • Chezmoi or Ansible: For managing local configurations and dotfiles without full OS-level functional programming, tools like Chezmoi bring templating and order to your user environment, while Ansible lets you write declarative YAML to control system states locally.

The Reality of the Chaos

The fundamental issue you pointed out is exactly right: you cannot unify the ecosystem. A higher language can only succeed if it acts as a robust orchestration layer.

If you want a shell that stops breaking because of string formatting variations, Nushell is worth a look. If you want a bulletproof foundation where you can leverage an entire ecosystem of stable libraries to do the heavy lifting instead of relying on fragile CLI utilities, migrating your complex automation logic to Python scripts wrapped with a setup harness is often the most stable path forward.

Do any of these particular angles—structured data, wrapping commands in a general-purpose language, or functional/declarative configuration—sound like the kind of leverage you are looking for?

turns.prompt_text: I think what I'm looking for specifically is the robustness, durability, and insurability of terminal commands, because I surely know exactly how they work, at least what they do. I want to be able to stand at a higher level and be able to come down to the terminal if I really need to. I'd like the best of both worlds. I really like elvish and nutshell. They look interesting to try out. Ansible also looks interesting. Essentially, what I'm looking for is a compiler
turns.response_html:
It sounds like you want a high-level, deterministic contract. You want a language that compiles down to the underlying system calls or commands, ensuring that what you wrote yesterday won't crumble tomorrow because a CLI tool shifted its flags or output format.

When you say you are looking for a compiler that gives you robustness and insurability while letting you drop down to the raw metal of the terminal when needed, you are describing a very specific philosophy in systems engineering.

Here is how that "compiler/translation layer" concept maps to the tools you liked, and where the ultimate version of this idea actually lives.

1. The Shell as a Transpiler (Nushell & Elvish)

If you think of standard shells as interpreters of raw strings, Nushell and Elvish act more like type-checked compiler front-ends.

  • The Insurability: They don't just execute a command; they enforce a data schema. When you pipe a command in Nushell, the shell "compiles" the output of the first command into an internal, structured table type before passing it to the next.
  • Dropping Down: If a structured tool fails or you need raw, unadulterated access to the underlying OS binaries, both shells allow you to bypass their internal type engines entirely (e.g., using ^command syntax in Nushell) to execute a raw terminal command exactly as you would in Fish or Bash.

2. The Idempotent Engine (Ansible)

Ansible functions essentially as a declarative-to-imperative compiler for system states.

  • The Insurability: You write highly structured YAML definitions of what the system should look like (e.g., "This file must exist with these permissions"). Ansible's engine "compiles" this abstract state into a series of highly robust, python-backed modules executed on the host system. It handles the edge cases, error states, and OS-specific translation for you.
  • Dropping Down: If Ansible's high-level abstractions don't cover a hyper-specific edge case, you don't have to rewrite the playbook. You simply drop down to the ansible.builtin.shell or command modules, which let you run raw, arbitrary terminal scripts right in the middle of your structured pipeline.

3. The Ultimate System Compiler: Nix

If you want a true compiler for your environment where the ground cannot break, Nix is the logical conclusion of your search.

Nix is a functional programming language designed to build and configure systems.

  • Pure Compilation: It takes your high-level configuration file, compiles it, and builds an entirely isolated, immutable environment. If you configure a tool via Nix, it locks down the exact binary version, its dependencies, and its environment variables. It is completely insurable—if it builds successfully once, it will build exactly the same way on any machine, forever.
  • Dropping Down: Because it's just managing the environment underneath, you open up a standard terminal and use your commands exactly as you always have. You retain 100% of your terminal mastery, but the foundation those tools stand on is frozen in carbonite until you explicitly choose to update the source code and re-compile.

Where to start?

If you want to change how you interact with the terminal day-to-day with a type-safe layer, drop Fish for a weekend and dive into Nushell.

If you want to change how you build and preserve your automation workflows so they never crumble, start looking into Ansible for local provisioning, or brave the steep learning curve of Nix for total system immutability.

Since you're looking for that compiler-like rigidity, which side of the coin feels more urgent to fix first: the interactive shell experience itself, or the stability of your automation scripts?
